blocks.text: India’s banking reforms were shaped largely by two committees that carry the same name, Narasimham. The **first (1991)** was about freeing banks from heavy controls; the **second (1998)** was about making the freed system stronger and safer.

blocks.title: How the Narasimham panels unfolded
items: Aug 1991
**Narasimham Committee I** is set up to study the problems of the Indian financial system and suggest ways to raise the efficiency and productivity of financial institutions.
**Narasimham Committee II** is set up.
Apr 1998
Committee II hands its report to the government.

blocks.title: Narasimham I (1991) vs Narasimham II (1998)
rows: Reduce the actual number of public sector banks
Strong banking system seen in the context of **Current Account Convertibility (CAC)**
Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) should focus on agriculture and rural financing
**Narrow Banking**: weak banks may place funds only in short-term, risk-free assets
Capital adequacy ratio to go up, not down
Government should **raise the prescribed capital adequacy norms** and urgently review and amend the main banking-sector laws

blocks.title: Other Narasimham I ideas that are asked in exams
items: Income recognition and asset classification norms for banks.
Setting up special tribunals (Debt Recovery Tribunals) so that recovery cases are settled faster.
Phasing out directed credit programmes, more autonomy to public sector banks, and a higher capital adequacy ratio (not a lower one).

blocks.title: Do not mix the two
blocks.text: SLR 25% and CRR 3.5% belong to Narasimham **I** (1991). Narrow Banking and Current Account Convertibility belong to Narasimham **II** (1998). Also remember that Narasimham I wanted capital adequacy to go up, not down.

blocks.title: Narasimham I: the two numbers
blocks.phrase: “Two-five and three-and-a-half”: SLR comes down to 25, CRR comes down to 3.5, in the year of liberalisation, 1991.
letters: Statutory Liquidity Ratio, to be reduced gradually to 25%
Cash Reserve Ratio, to be reduced gradually to 3.5%
blocks.note: Think of SLR as the bigger bucket (25) and CRR as the smaller bucket (3.5).

blocks.title: Narasimham II: what is ‘narrow’?
blocks.phrase: Weak bank, Narrow path: a weak bank walks only on a narrow, safe path, short-term and risk-free assets, while the whole system prepares for CAC.
letters: Capital adequacy norms to be raised
Laws of banking to be reviewed and amended

sections.title: Damodaran, Usha Thorat and M V Nair (2011)

blocks.text: Three RBI-linked committees of 2011 are exam favourites. Each looked at a different corner of the system: **customers**, **NBFCs** and **priority sector lending**.

blocks.title: Damodaran Committee, 2011
rows: M. Damodaran, former Chairman of SEBI.
Look into customer service issues and evaluate the existing grievance redressal mechanism in banks.
Banks should offer **No Frill Savings Accounts** with basic facilities such as a cheque book and an ATM card, **without any minimum balance**.
**No liability on the customer** for losses in ATM and online transactions.

blocks.title: Usha Thorat Committee, 2011
rows: Usha Thorat, Director of the Centre for Advanced Financial Research and Learning (CAFRAL).
Presented its suggestions on **29 August 2011**; an **8-member** panel.
Non-Banking Finance Companies (NBFCs); it also examined issues related to offshore rupee markets and recommended policy measures.
A higher capital norm of **12%** for NBFCs, with asset classification and provisioning on the lines of banks.
Minimum asset size of over **₹50 crore** to register a new NBFC.
NBFCs that do not access public funds and have assets below **₹1,000 crore** are exempt from registration.

blocks.title: M V Nair Committee, 2011
rows: By the Reserve Bank on **25 August 2011**, following an announcement in the Monetary Policy Statement 2011-12.
Re-examine the existing classification and suggest revised guidelines on **priority sector lending** and related issues.

blocks.title: One line each
blocks.text: Damodaran = customer service and grievances. Usha Thorat = NBFCs (12% capital, ₹50 crore, ₹1,000 crore). M V Nair = priority sector lending classification.

blocks.title: The 2011 trio: D-T-N
blocks.phrase: Dam the complaints (Damodaran), Thorat’s NBFC Throne, Nair needs Priority.
letters: Damodaran: customer service and grievance redressal, no-frill accounts
Thorat: NBFCs, 12% capital, ₹50 crore minimum asset size
blocks.note: A dam holds back a flood of complaints, which is how Damodaran helps customers.

blocks.text: The RBI appointed a committee on **comprehensive financial services for small businesses and low-income households** in **September 2013**, under Nachiket Mor, a member of RBI’s Central Board of Directors.

blocks.title: Main recommendations
items: Every adult (above 18 years) should have a bank account by **1 January 2016**. This account would be called the **Universal Electronic Bank Account (UEBA)**.
A bank should itself issue an account to every resident at the time the person receives an **Aadhaar number** (UIDAI).
Set up **payments banks**.
Abolish the **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** gradually and introduce the **Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)** under **Basel III** norms.

blocks.title: Niche banks too
blocks.text: In an exam-style item, the external advisory committee that reported to the RBI on the first-ever niche banking licences was also headed by Nachiket Mor. Payments banks and small finance banks are the niche banks.

blocks.title: Mor = MORE accounts
blocks.phrase: MOR means MORE accounts: every adult gets one by 1-1-2016, a UEBA, handed over along with Aadhaar.
letters: Millions of adults: all above 18 years
One account each, the Universal Electronic Bank Account (UEBA)
Resident gets it when Aadhaar is issued
blocks.note: Date check: 1 January 2016. Liquidity check: SLR out slowly, LCR in (Basel III).

sections.title: U K Sinha Committee, Video KYC and KYC rules

blocks.text: The **Upendra Kumar Sinha Committee (2019)** was an expert committee on **MSMEs**, headed by U K Sinha, a former Chairman of SEBI. It recommended that the RBI introduce **video KYC** in place of the current KYC methods.

blocks.title: How video KYC works
items: The customer opens or updates the account without visiting a branch.
A bank officer joins through a video call.
The customer’s KYC documents are verified during the call.
The customer’s signature is recorded on video.
The whole process can be done within a few minutes.

blocks.title: How often must KYC be refreshed? (guidelines issued 23 July 2013)
KYC milestones
items: RBI issues the revised guidelines with risk-based KYC timelines.
U K Sinha Committee recommends video KYC.

Because of the COVID-19 pandemic, RBI rationalises some KYC norms: limited KYC accounts can be converted into full KYC accounts, and video KYC is allowed for customers in small businesses and legal entities.

blocks.title: Check what changes with risk
blocks.text: The riskier the customer, the shorter the gap: 2 years for high risk, 8 for medium, 10 for low. Exams may swap the numbers, so recall the order high to low risk as 2, 8, 10.

blocks.title: KYC gaps: 2-8-10
blocks.phrase: High risk, Hurry: 2. Medium risk, Mid-way: 8. Low risk, Long wait: 10. The gaps grow as the risk falls.

blocks.title: Committee and what it is known for
rows: Its recommendations led to **Universal Banking** being implemented in India.
Reported to the RBI on the first niche banking licences; also the 2013 financial-inclusion committee.

Reviews, simplifies and rewrites the laws affecting financial markets; evolves common governance principles for financial regulators; streamlines the regulatory architecture. It was formed in **2011**, not 2013.
RBI-linked panel on **MSME** reforms (also video KYC).
Reviewed the regulatory and supervisory framework for **Core Investment Companies (CICs)**.
11-member committee headed by a former Finance Secretary, on **incentivising transactions through cards and digital** means.
Studied **household finance** in India, including households’ demand for assets such as pensions and for liabilities.
Suggested initiatives on the **medium-term path for financial inclusion**.
Committee on **Financial Inclusion**, set up in **2006**.
Set up in **2004** to prepare a report on financial inclusion.
Review of the **governance of boards** of banks in India.
Income recognition and asset classification norms; Debt Recovery Tribunals and special tribunals for faster settlement of cases.

revision: Narasimham I (Aug 1991): reduce SLR gradually to 25% and CRR to 3.5%; fewer PSBs; RRBs to focus on agriculture and rural finance.
Narasimham II was set up on 26 Dec 1997 and reported in April 1998: Narrow Banking, Current Account Convertibility, higher capital adequacy norms.
Damodaran Committee (2011): customer service and grievances; no-frill account without minimum balance; no customer liability for ATM or online losses.
Usha Thorat Committee (29 Aug 2011): 12% capital for NBFCs; minimum asset size over ₹50 crore; exemption below ₹1,000 crore without public funds.
M V Nair Committee (25 Aug 2011): classification and guidelines on priority sector lending.
Nachiket Mor (Sept 2013): every adult above 18 to have an account by 1 Jan 2016 (UEBA); payments banks; abolish SLR, adopt LCR under Basel III.
U K Sinha Committee (2019, MSMEs): recommended video KYC in place of present KYC methods.
KYC refresh: high risk every 2 years, medium risk every 8 years, low risk every 10 years (guidelines of 23 July 2013).
On 5 May 2021, because of COVID-19, RBI allowed conversion of limited KYC to full KYC and video KYC for small businesses and legal entities.
R H Khan Committee led to Universal Banking in India; Tapan Ray looked at Core Investment Companies; Ratan P Watal at digital payments.
FSLRC reviews and rewrites financial laws and was formed in 2011 (not 2013); Shivaraman Committee led to the creation of NABARD.
Financial inclusion committees: Khan (2004), C Rangarajan (2006), Nachiket Mor (2013), Deepak Mohanty (medium-term path).
P J Nayak examined governance of bank boards; Tarun Ramadorai studied household finance in India.
Wanchoo and Chesi dealt with direct taxes; L K Jha and Rekhi with indirect taxes; Urjit Patel with the monetary policy framework.
